# Plan — `entire handoff` with a Databricks export lane (3 people)

## Context

`docs-private/IMPLEMENTATION_ROADMAP.md` is a live buildathon roadmap for **Track E1**: a new
`entire handoff` command producing a *verifiable handoff packet* for AI coding sessions — every line
carrying a checkpoint citation. Submission is **15:00 IST**; it is now **~10:52**, `cmd/entire/cli/handoff/`
does not exist, and **M1 (contract pushed) is 11:05**.

I verified the roadmap against the source. **Its technical content is accurate** — `GetCompactTranscriptStart() (offset int, ok bool)`
(`api/checkpoint/metadata.go:503`), the `Summary` fields (`metadata.go:595-601`), `PersistentStore`
(`api/checkpoint/interfaces.go:13-34`), `checkpoint.Open(...)` (`cmd/entire/cli/resume.go:198`),
`newRecapCmd()` (`root.go:198`), `"recap"` (`agent_help_cmd.go:142`), and `writeManagedScaffold` /
`openScaffoldRoot` (`setup_managed_scaffold.go:67,105`) all exist exactly as described. Build on it.

Three things in it are **wrong or missing**, and this plan corrects them:

1. **Databricks is listed as cut** (`IMPLEMENTATION_ROADMAP.md:641`). The user has reaffirmed it is
   **in scope**, so this plan un-cuts it as **Workstream D**.
2. **§0 / §0.1 does not exist** — cited at lines 5 and 641, but the doc starts at §1. The
   justification for the Databricks cut is simply absent, which is part of why overriding it is safe.
3. **`BUILD_RULES.md`, `APPLICATION_ANSWER.md`, `IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md` do not exist.**
   `docs-private/` contains only the roadmap. Every brief must therefore **inline** its rules rather
   than cite those files.

### The cost of un-cutting Databricks — stated plainly

The roadmap is a 3-person A/B/C split. Adding Databricks with the same headcount takes one person off
the core product. Workstream C (sections 1/2/5, the managed skill, graph evidence) becomes unowned.

**I absorb C.** I own A + C; the two agents own B and D. The dead-end miner (B) stays with a dedicated
person because the roadmap is right that it is the differentiator — it is the only thing `entire handoff`
does that the already-shipped `session-handoff` skill does not.

---

## Role mapping

| Who | Workstream | Owns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Me (main)** | **A + C** | contract, spine, `input.go`, renderers, registration, stubs, sections 1/2/5, managed skill, **integration + merges** |
| **Person A** | **D — Databricks** | packet export to Databricks + warehouse-side Delta/SQL assets |
| **Person B** | **B — CLI dead-end miner** | `transcript.go`, `deadends.go`, fixture, tests |

---

## The contract (frozen — §3 of the roadmap, verbatim)

`cmd/entire/cli/handoff/packet.go` is written by me and **frozen after 11:00**. Both agents code
against §3 of the roadmap *immediately*, without waiting for the file.

The invariant everything is judged on: **every `Item` carries ≥1 `Citation`.** I own the test that
enforces it across all extractors (`packet_test.go`).

**Failure is a `Note`, not an `error`.** An extractor that cannot do its job returns an empty
`Items` + populated `Note` + `nil` error. Partial packets are the product.

**Stdlib only. No new `go.mod`/`go.sum` entries.** This binds Workstream D too — no Databricks SDK.

---

## Workstream D — Databricks (Person A)

Deliberately designed so it is **genuinely parallel**, not fake-parallel.

**Two tiers.** Tier 1 is Go in this repo; Tier 2 is pure Databricks-side and touches no Go at all.

- **Tier 1 — `cmd/entire/cli/handoff/export_databricks.go`** (sole owner: Person A).
  `ExportPacket(ctx, p Packet) error` uploads the packet JSON to a Unity Catalog **Volume** via the
  Files API — `PUT /api/2.0/fs/files/{path}`, `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, stdlib `net/http`.
  Chosen over the SQL Statement Execution API on purpose: no SQL string-escaping, no injection
  surface, ~80 lines.
- **Tier 2 — `databricks/` notebook + DDL** (zero Go): `COPY INTO` / Auto Loader from the volume into
  a Delta table `handoff_packets`, plus 2–3 analytics SQL queries (dead ends per repo, open items
  aging). **100% independent of the CLI** — buildable and demoable even if Tier 1 slips.

**Credentials rule (non-negotiable, from this repo's `CLAUDE.md`).** Config comes from **environment
variables only** — `DATABRICKS_HOST`, `DATABRICKS_TOKEN`, `DATABRICKS_VOLUME_PATH`. It must **not** go
into `.entire/settings.json`, which is version-controlled; a token there ships to everyone who clones.
This also sidesteps the `enforce*Trust` machinery (`settings/opf_command_trust.go`,
`settings/external_agents_trust.go`) entirely — no trust gate to build.

**Honest dependency accounting** (the brief will say this in its own "Blocked by" section):
- ✅ Independent: the uploader is a pure function of `Packet`. Person A tests it against a
  hand-written `Packet` literal + `httptest.Server`. **No checkpoints, no git, no agent needed.**
- ⚠️ Compile-blocked until M1, exactly like Workstream B. Writing can start now; `go build` cannot.
- ⚠️ **One wiring line in `handoff.go` (my file).** I stub `--export-databricks` at M1 so Person A
  never opens my file. Same stub trick the roadmap uses for `extractors.go`.
- ⚠️ Tier 2 needs a real Databricks workspace + a UC volume. **If there is no workspace, Tier 1
  still ships and writes to a local dir via `DATABRICKS_HOST=file://…`** — that fallback is required,
  not optional, so the demo cannot hard-depend on network access.

**Also assigned to Person A:** graph evidence #1 and #2 (15 scored points). They have genuine slack
before M1 while I write the contract, and the artefacts are quick commands. Details in the brief.

## Workstream B — dead-end miner (Person B)

Roadmap §4.2, essentially unchanged; it is already correct and verified.

- `transcript.go` — own line parser. **Do not use `compact.BuildCondensedEntries`**: it builds `tool`
  entries from `block["name"]`/`block["input"]` only and never reads `block["result"]`
  (`transcript/compact/parse.go:88-105`), so the error status is invisible to it. The status *is* on
  disk — `compact.go:476` writes `blocks[idx]["result"]` and `buildToolResult` sets `Status: "error"`.
- `deadends.go` — group by `input.command` / `input.file_path` / tool name; count, first line offset,
  error output **truncated to ~200 chars** (a security requirement — transcripts can contain pasted
  tokens), plus the following assistant text (the highest-value string in the packet).
- **Slicing trap:** use `CompactStart`/`HasCompactStart` from `Input`; `HasCompactStart == false`
  means legacy → line 0. Never `GetTranscriptStart()` (different coordinate system). Tolerate one
  repeated head line.
- **Go/no-go first:** grep a real transcript for `"status":"error"`. If 0, report immediately — the
  feature changes shape.

---

## Files I will create

entire handoff            # human-readable markdown
entire handoff --json     # machine-readable "handoff packet"
```

session made. Today the only fix is a human pasting context by hand.

**The product.** `entire handoff` reads the repo's Entire checkpoints and emits a *verifiable* packet

central claim is that **every line carries a checkpoint citation**, so nothing in the packet is an
unattributable assertion by a language model. A fresh agent runs one command and is oriented.

**Your lane** turns that packet into a durable, queryable, cross-session memory in Databricks. The CLI
answers *"what happened in this repo recently?"*. Your lane answers **"has anyone on this team ever
tried this before, and did it fail?"** — across every repo and every session, not just the local clone.

That retrieval claim is the reason Workstream D exists. It is not analytics decoration.

## §1 — What we are building (context)

We are adding a command to the Entire CLI:

```
entire handoff            # human-readable markdown
entire handoff --json     # machine-readable "handoff packet"

**The problem.** When an AI coding session ends, the next session starts blind. It re-tries approaches
that already failed, re-asks answered questions, and silently drops promises. Today the only fix is a
human pasting context by hand.

**The product.** `entire handoff` reads the repo's Entire checkpoints and emits a *verifiable* packet
in five sections — **intent, open items, dead ends, surface (blast radius), where it stopped**. The
central claim is that **every line carries a checkpoint citation**.

### Why your workstream is the one that matters

Entire already ships an official `session-handoff` skill that summarises sessions. The obvious
criticism of this whole project is **"isn't this just a wrapper around that?"**

**Your miner is the answer.** Sections 1, 2 and 5 read summaries that already exist. Yours reads
transcript internals that **no CLI command and no exported helper exposes today** — the
`result.status` of every tool call — and mines the failures. "Three sessions ago someone tried
`go test -run TestRecap` and it failed with `undefined: recapFlags`" is not something the existing
skill can say. That is the differentiator, and it is why you get a dedicated person.

---

`transcript.jsonl`.** Verify it before investing an hour.

```bash
entire enable -y --agent claude-code

# Make one throwaway commit whose session contains a DELIBERATELY FAILING tool call,
# e.g. ask the agent to run:  cat /nope
git log -1 --format=%B                     # must show an "Entire-Checkpoint:" trailer
entire checkpoint list

git cat-file -p refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>    # must contain 0/transcript.jsonl
grep -c '"status":"error"' <that transcript>

**Report that number out loud immediately.**

is to mine `Summary.Friction` text instead, which is a much weaker product, and the integrator needs
to know within minutes, not at noon.

```go

type Citation struct {
    CheckpointID string `json:"checkpoint_id"`
    SessionIndex int    `json:"session_index"`
    Line         int    `json:"line,omitempty"` // transcript.jsonl offset; dead ends only
}

type Item struct {
    Text  string     `json:"text"`
    Cites []Citation `json:"cites"`
}

    Name  string `json:"name"`
    Items []Item `json:"items"`
    Note  string `json:"note,omitempty"`
}

type Checkpoint struct {
    ID           string
    SessionIndex int
    CreatedAt    time.Time
    Metadata     *apicheckpoint.Metadata // never nil

}

    Repo        string
    Head        string

}

    Name() string
    Extract(ctx context.Context, in Input) (Section, error)
}
```

**Two rules every extractor obeys:**

1. **Every `Item` carries at least one `Citation`.** This is the product's central claim. The
   integrator owns a test that enforces it mechanically across all extractors. An uncited item is a bug.
2. **Failure is a `Note`, not an `error`.** If you cannot do your job, return a `Section` with empty

   worse than useless at noon.

```json
{"v":1,"agent":"claude-code","cli_version":"0.42.0","type":"assistant","ts":"…","id":"msg_x",
 "content":[{"type":"text","text":"…"},
            {"type":"tool_use","id":"…","name":"Bash","input":{…},
             "result":{"output":"…","status":"error"}}]}
```

```go
type toolCall struct {
    Line   int    // offset in transcript.jsonl — becomes Citation.Line
    Name   string
    Input  map[string]any
    Status string // "success" | "error" | ""
    Output string
}

func scanToolCalls(transcript []byte, from int) ([]toolCall, []string, error)
```

- Split on `\n`; `json.Unmarshal` each line into `{Type string; Content json.RawMessage}`.
- **Skip blank and unparseable lines — never fail the command on one bad line.**
- For `type == "assistant"`, unmarshal `Content` into `[]map[string]json.RawMessage`; for blocks with

Adds `entire handoff` / `entire handoff --json`, which reads the repo's

Workstream A+C of the three-way split. Lands the frozen contract so the

Design decisions:

- Extractor seam plus stubs.go: each section is one file with one constructor,
  so a new section (including one a curveball demands) is a new file and a
  stub deletion. No shared file is edited twice, which is what keeps three
  branches from colliding on the wiring.
- Failure is a Note, not an error. A section that cannot do its job returns
  empty Items with a reason and a nil error. Partial packets are the product:
  a packet that refuses to print because one section degraded is worse than
  useless to the agent that needs orienting.
- CompactStart is resolved once in input.go. GetTranscriptStart indexes raw
  full.jsonl and GetCompactTranscriptStart indexes transcript.jsonl; mixing
  them yields citations that point at the wrong line while still looking
  valid, so no extractor calls either method itself.
- Open items are annotated "(likely closed)", never deleted. A silently
  dropped promise is the exact failure this command exists to fix, so the
  heuristic may add a hint but never remove a line.
- Empty-range note names checkpoints, not summaries. Blaming summaries when
  there was nothing to read sends the reader after a problem they don't have.
- RenderJSON normalises nil slices to []. The JSON shape is consumed by other
  tools, and a null where an array was expected breaks the parser on exactly
  the packet with an empty section.
- agent-help classified read-only + unlisted. Read-only is defensible since
  handoff writes nothing; unlisted is the safe default, because promoting a
  command into the advertised listing changes what agents run unprompted in
  every user's repo and is a call for a human to make.

-- Storage for `entire handoff --json` packets.
--
-- Merge key is (repo_key, checkpoint_id, session_id) -- never repo_key alone.
-- A repo without a remote gets a synthetic `local/<basename>` key, so two
-- developers' local clones collide on `local/cli`. Row-level uniqueness needs
-- section_name and item_index on top of the merge key, because one checkpoint
-- contributes many rows.
--
-- item_index = -1 marks a section that produced no items; section_note then
-- carries the reason it degraded. Those rows are kept deliberately: "the graph
-- was degenerate" is itself a finding, and dropping them makes an empty
-- section indistinguishable from one that was never run.

CREATE VOLUME IF NOT EXISTS main.default.handoff
  COMMENT 'Landing zone for handoff packet NDJSON uploaded by handoff-databricks.';

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS main.default.handoff_packets (
  repo_key           STRING  NOT NULL COMMENT 'Packet repo field; may be local/<basename> and is NOT unique on its own',
  checkpoint_id      STRING           COMMENT 'Cited checkpoint; empty for item_index = -1 rows',
  session_id         INT              COMMENT 'Session index within the checkpoint',
  head_checkpoint_id STRING           COMMENT 'HEAD Entire-Checkpoint trailer at generation time',
  generated_at       TIMESTAMP        COMMENT 'When the packet was produced',
  section_name       STRING  NOT NULL COMMENT 'intent | open_items | dead_ends | surface | stopped',
  item_index         INT     NOT NULL COMMENT '-1 when the section was empty',
  item_text          STRING           COMMENT 'The cited line',
  cite_line          INT              COMMENT 'transcript.jsonl offset; dead_ends only',
  section_note       STRING           COMMENT 'Degradation reason when the section is empty',
  ingested_at        TIMESTAMP        COMMENT 'Ingest time, set by the uploader'
)
USING DELTA
PARTITIONED BY (repo_key)
COMMENT 'Handoff packets, one row per (section, item, citation).';

-- Vector Search source view: the two sections worth retrieving across repos.
-- Citation columns are carried through on purpose -- a retrieval result without
-- a checkpoint id is the unverifiable assertion the packet exists to avoid.
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW main.default.handoff_retrievable AS
SELECT
  repo_key,
  checkpoint_id,
  session_id,
  cite_line,
  section_name,
  item_text,
  generated_at
FROM main.default.handoff_packets
WHERE section_name IN ('dead_ends', 'intent')
  AND item_index >= 0
  AND item_text IS NOT NULL;

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

Design plan before I build:

**Color** — cool paper `#FCFCFD` / ink `#15191F`, cool grey-blue muted `#616C7C`, petrol `#0E6E6B` as the single accent carrying "added by us", neutral grey `#8A93A3` for "pre-existing", ochre `#9A5410` for caveats. Provenance is the subject, so the palette does semantic work rather than decoration.
**Type** — system grotesque for headings (tight tracking), serif for running prose (the non-technical narrative needs to read like prose, not UI), mono for paths and commands.
**Layout** — single column at ~68ch for prose, full-bleed scrollable containers for the diagrams, a persistent ADDED/EXISTING legend so the distinction holds across every section.

Architecture & high-level design

entire handoff

A cited briefing that lets one coding session pick up exactly where the last one stopped — including the things that were already tried and failed.

Built by us Already existed

What we are building, in plain terms

When someone works with an AI assistant on a piece of software, every new conversation starts from nothing. The assistant has no memory of yesterday. So it suggests an approach that was already tried and abandoned last week, asks a question that was answered on Tuesday, and quietly forgets the three things it promised to come back to. The only fix available today is a person sitting down and re-explaining the situation by hand, from memory, every single time — and people are bad at remembering which of five approaches was the one that didn't work.

The tool this repository already provides quietly records each of those working sessions as it happens, the way a flight recorder does. Nobody reads those recordings, because they are enormous and unreadable. What we built is the thing that reads them for you. Type one command and you get a short briefing: what the last sessions were trying to achieve, what was left unfinished, what was already attempted and failed, which parts of the system were disturbed, and where work stopped mid-sentence.

The part that matters most is the smallest. Every single line in that briefing is stamped with the recording it came from. So none of it is the assistant guessing or embellishing — each claim can be traced back to the moment it actually happened, and checked. A briefing you cannot verify is just a rumour with better formatting.

We then send those briefings to a shared company database. That turns a personal memory aid into an institutional one: instead of only knowing what you tried last Tuesday, anyone can ask whether anybody has attempted this before and how it went. The failures stop being wasted.

System flow

Grey is the platform that already existed; teal is what we added. Note that we consume the existing recording pipeline without modifying any part of it.

# `entire handoff` — architecture and high-level design A cited briefing that lets one coding session pick up exactly where the last one stopped, including the things that were already tried and failed. Throughout this document: - **ADDED** — built for this feature. - **EXISTED** — pre-existing platform we consume without modifying. --- ## What we are building, in plain terms When someone works with an AI assistant on a piece of software, every new conversation starts from nothing. The assistant has no memory of yesterday. So it suggests an approach that was already tried and abandoned last week, asks a question that was answered on Tuesday, and quietly forgets the three things it promised to come back to. The only fix available today is a person sitting down and re-explaining the situation by hand, from memory, every single time — and people are bad at remembering which of five approaches was the one that did not work. The tool this repository already provides quietly records each of those working sessions as it happens, the way a flight recorder does. Nobody reads those recordings, because they are enormous and unreadable. What we built is the thing that reads them for you. Type one command and you get a short briefing: what the last sessions were trying to achieve, what was left unfinished, *what was already attempted and failed*, which parts of the system were disturbed, and where work stopped mid-sentence. The part that matters most is the smallest. Every single line in that briefing is stamped with the recording it came from. So none of it is the assistant guessing or embellishing — each claim can be traced back to the moment it actually happened, and checked. A briefing you cannot verify is just a rumour with better formatting. We then send those briefings to a shared company database. That turns a personal memory aid into an institutional one: instead of only knowing what *you* tried last Tuesday, anyone can ask whether *anybody* has attempted this before and how it went. To open the session behind any claim: ```bash entire checkpoint explain ``` A section may be empty with a note explaining why. That is normal and deliberate — partial packets are the product. --- ## Data contract `entire handoff --json` emits this shape. It is a published interface: the managed skill and the Databricks lane both depend on it. Adding a field is safe; renaming or removing one is a breaking change for both. ```json { "repo": "gh/acme/cli", "generated_at": "2026-09-06T10:40:00Z", "head_checkpoint_id": "01JQ8Z9K2M3N4P5Q6R7S8T9V0W", "sections": [ { "name": "dead_ends", "items": [ { "text": "go test ./... -run TestRecap — failed 2 times: undefined: recapFlags", "cites": [ { "checkpoint_id": "01JQ8Z9K…", "session_index": 0, "line": 412 } ] } ] }, { "name": "surface", "items": [], "note": "graph degenerate: no_dependents" } ] } ``` Section names are part of the contract: `intent`, `open_items`, `dead_ends`, `surface`, `stopped`. `line` is populated only by the dead-end miner, which is the one extractor working at line granularity. ### Warehouse schema One packet becomes N rows, one per `(section, item, citation)`. The section discloses this in its own output. - **Blast radius is untested against live graph output.** It is covered only by an injected fake, so the real `entire graph diff` field names are an informed guess. A mismatch degrades to the touched-file list rather than breaking. - **Tool output is truncated to ~200 characters.** A security measure, not formatting — transcripts can contain a pasted credential. --- ## Verification ```bash go build ./... # clean go vet ./cmd/entire/cli/handoff/... ./cmd/handoff-databricks/... gofmt -l cmd/entire/cli/handoff/ cmd/handoff-databricks/ golangci-lint run ./cmd/entire/cli/handoff/... ./cmd/handoff-databricks/... go test ./cmd/entire/cli/... ./cmd/handoff-databricks/... ``` The dead-end miner is additionally verified against `cmd/entire/cli/transcript/compact/testdata/claude_expected2.jsonl` — the compact writer's own committed expected output, which contains four real `status:"error"` blocks. Yes — any semantic search means embedding the text. But the two options differ in a way that matters.

## What we'd be embedding

Our `item_text` comes from two places:
- **intent / open_items** — `Summary.*`, model-generated summaries.
- **dead_ends** — the command, plus tool error output truncated to 200 chars, plus the assistant's follow-up text.

`dead_ends` is the sensitive one. Truncation is a mitigation, not a guarantee — an AWS key is 20 chars and fits comfortably inside 200.

## The protection is upstream, and it already exists

What saves this is that **we never read raw transcripts.** Per the pipeline in `CLAUDE.md`, every stored transcript is sanitized → image-externalized → **redacted** before the checkpoint blob is written. `ReadSessionContent` hands us the already-redacted bytes. So the text we'd embed has been through the betterleaks ruleset and the entropy layer.

That's best-effort pattern matching, not a proof — but it's the same content the platform already stores and pushes, so we're not lowering the bar.

## Where the two options genuinely differ

| | `entire search` | Databricks Vector Search |
|---|---|---|
| Where embedding happens | Server-side, in entire-api cells | In your Databricks workspace |
| What leaves your machine | **The query string only** | **The corpus** — every dead end and intent |
| New data exposure | **None** — checkpoints were already pushed and indexed | **Yes** — a new copy to a third party |

`search_v4.go` confirms it: the CLI holds no embedder. It resolves repos through the control plane and fans out a *query* to cells (`fanOutCells`, line 173). The corpus is already there because `entire/checkpoints/v1` gets pushed as part of normal operation.

So option 3 embeds nothing new — the indexing already happened, on data you already sent. Option 2 is the one that creates a second copy of transcript-derived text in a system with its own access model, retention, and audit story.

That's an argument for option 3 on privacy grounds, and it's worth saying plainly: **the Databricks lane's value isn't retrieval quality, it's cross-team institutional memory in a warehouse you control.** If retrieval is the goal, `entire search` gets there with less exposure and no workspace.

## What "embedding" means here

To search by meaning (not just exact words), a computer has to read all your text and convert it into numbers. That's embedding. So yes — either way, something reads the text.

## Right now we do none of it

What we built only matches text exactly. If one session ran `go test ./...` and another ran `go test -v ./...`, we treat those as two unrelated things. No meaning-based matching anywhere.

## The worry is fair

The riskiest text is the failure messages, because error output sometimes contains a password or key someone pasted. I cut that output to 200 characters, but that doesn't really solve it — a key is short enough to survive the cut.

**The real protection already exists and isn't ours.** Before Entire saves any recording, it scans it and strips out things that look like secrets. We only ever read the already-cleaned version. It's a filter, not a guarantee — but it's the same cleaning the tool already does for everything else.

## The actual difference between the two options

**Using Entire's own search:** your recordings are *already* on Entire's servers — that's just how the tool works. They've already been read and indexed. So if you search, you're only sending a question. Nothing new leaves your computer.

**Using Databricks:** you'd be making a **second copy** of that text and sending it somewhere new. That's a genuinely new exposure — a different company, different access rules, different retention.

## So

If you want meaning-based search, Entire's existing search is the safer path: nothing new leaves, and it needs no Databricks account.

The Databricks piece is still worth having — but not for search quality. It's worth it because it puts your team's history in a database *you* control, where anyone can ask "has someone here hit this before?" That's the reason to keep it, and it's an honest one.

## None of today's work was captured by Entire

**`.git/hooks/` is empty** — no Entire hooks were ever installed in this clone. `entire status` says "Enabled" because `.entire/settings.json` says so, but the hooks that actually create checkpoints aren't there.

The 100 checkpoints `entire checkpoint list` shows are inherited upstream history from `entireio/cli` (dated 09-04), not ours.

For the buildathon this matters: checkpoint quality is 15 points and four checkpoints are a required artifact. Right now none exist for this work.

## I also found a real bug in my own code

`entire handoff` prints **"no checkpoints in range"** while 100 checkpoints exist. They're unhydrated remote stubs, and my `loadCheckpoint` skips anything whose `ReadSessionContent` fails — silently. So on a fresh clone, which is exactly the demo scenario, the command claims there's nothing when there are 100. It should say "100 checkpoints found, none readable — try `entire checkpoint list`". That's my mistake and I should fix it.

## To actually make a checkpoint

Checkpoints aren't created by a direct command — `entire checkpoint` only has `list`/`explain`/`tokens`/`search`, and `entire hooks` is internal. One is produced by: **hooks installed → agent session does work → commit → post-commit condenses it.**

So it needs `entire enable` to install the hooks. That writes into `.git/hooks/` and may touch agent config, which is why I'm asking rather than just running it.

## Fixed

**Root cause found.** The hooks were installed all along, but every invocation printed *"Entire CLI is enabled but not installed or not on PATH"* and silently exited. The `entire` binary only existed at `/tmp/entire`, which I'd built. I installed it to `~/.local/bin/entire` and symlinked it into `/usr/local/bin`, which is on PATH. `git log -1` still shows **no `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer**, and `entire session list` still says **No sessions**.

A commit does not create a checkpoint by itself. Checkpoints capture *agent session activity* — the Claude Code hooks fire on each turn, build session state, and the post-commit hook then condenses that state into a checkpoint. With no session state, there is nothing to condense, so the hook correctly does nothing.

The Claude Code hooks are configured in `.claude/settings.json` (I can see `entire hooks claude-code post-task` / `post-todo`), **but this session was already running before they became live.** A process doesn't pick up hook config mid-flight.

**Restart your Claude Code session.** The next one will fire hooks from its first turn, build session state, and every commit after that will carry a trailer and mint a checkpoint. That is the only path — I can't retroactively manufacture a checkpoint for work that was never recorded.

# Status: what was built, what was skipped, where we diverged

Accounting against `IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md` (Steps 0–11) and
`IMPLEMENTATION_ROADMAP.md` (M0–M5). Written after the fact from the actual
tree, not from intent.

---

## 1. What exists

**One new command**, `entire handoff` / `entire handoff --json`, producing a
five-section cited packet. All five sections implemented; no stubs remain.

**One new binary**, `cmd/handoff-databricks`, consuming packet JSON on stdin and
writing warehouse rows.

**One managed skill**, installed by `entire enable --handoff-skill`, telling a
fresh agent to run the command before reading any file.

| Area | Files |
| --- | --- |
| Command | `cmd/entire/cli/handoff.go` |
| Package | `handoff/`: `packet.go` `input.go` `build.go` `extractors.go` `intent.go` `openitems.go` `transcript.go` `deadends.go` `surface.go` `stopped.go` `render_md.go` `render_json.go` |
| Tests | `packet_test.go` `input_test.go` `deadends_test.go` `surface_test.go` `transcript_realdata_test.go` — **47 test functions** total |
| Skill | `cmd/entire/cli/setup_handoff_skill.go` |
| Warehouse | `cmd/handoff-databricks/{main,rows,upload}.go` + `upload_test.go`, `databricks/ddl.sql` |
| Docs | `docs/architecture/handoff.md`, two workstream briefs in `docs-private/` |
| Registration | 4 one-line edits: `root.go`, `agent_help_cmd.go`, `setup.go`, `root_test.go` |

Quality gates: `go build ./...` clean, `go vet` clean, `gofmt` clean,
`golangci-lint` clean on all new and changed files, full `./cmd/entire/cli/...`
and `./cmd/handoff-databricks/...` suites green.

**No existing behaviour was changed.** Every pre-existing component is read-only
from our side.

---

## 2. Plan step → outcome

| Step | Planned | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | Fork → mirror → clone → enable → go/no-go grep | **Diverged.** No fork or mirror; worked in the existing clone. Go/no-go answered differently — see §3.1 |
| 1 | Walking skeleton, registered, printing | **Done** |
| 2 | Packet type + extractor seam | **Done**, with contract additions — §3.4 |
| 3 | Sections 1, 2, 5 | **Done** |
| 4 | Dead-end miner | **Done** — the differentiator |
| 5 | Section 4, blast radius | **Done**, different mechanism — §3.2 |
| 6 | Renderers + stable commit | **Done** |
| 7 | Managed skill | **Done** |
| 8 | Noon curveball protocol | **Not applicable** — no curveball was issued |
| 9 | MCP tool (optional) | **Not built.** `grep entire_handoff cmd/entire/cli/mcp.go` → 0 |
| 10 | Databricks lane (stretch) | **Partial** — Tier 1 only, §3.5 |
| 11 | `BUILDATHON.md` + submit | **Not done.** File does not exist |

---

## 3. Divergences, with reasons

### 3.1 Go/no-go was answered from committed fixtures, not a live session

The plan called for making a throwaway commit with a deliberately failing tool
call, then grepping the resulting transcript for `"status":"error"`.

Instead the answer came from
`cmd/entire/cli/transcript/compact/testdata/claude_expected2.jsonl` — the compact
writer's own committed expected output, which contains **4 real
`status:"error"` blocks**. This is stronger evidence than a one-off live run,
and `transcript_realdata_test.go` now asserts against it continuously, so the
test fails if the writer format and our parser ever diverge.

### 3.2 `graph diff`, not `graph impact`

The plan said: for each file, run `entire graph impact`.

That cannot work. `impact` **requires `--symbol`**, and what a checkpoint carries
is `FilesTouched` — paths, not symbols. `surface.go` uses `entire graph diff`,
which returns entity-level changes with `dependents_count` and needs no symbol
input. Degenerate entities are suppressed rather than dressed up.

### 3.3 Three factual errors in the source documents

| Claim | Reality |
| --- | --- |
| `IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md:37` — build "needs CGO for tree-sitter" | No tree-sitter in `go.mod`. No CGO required |
| Plan code samples use go-git **v5** | This repo is on **v6**. First build failed on the v5 import |
| `ROADMAP §6` — "exactly four" conflict points | **Five.** `root_test.go` holds a second group table; `TestRoot_VisibleCommandsAreGrouped` failed until `handoff` was added to it |

`ROADMAP` also cites `§0.1` for the Databricks cut, and cites `§0` in its header
— **§0 does not exist in that file.** `BUILD_RULES.md`, `APPLICATION_ANSWER.md`,
`IDEAS.md`, and `docs/snapshot-format.md` are referenced throughout and none
exist, which is why both workstream briefs inline their rules.

### 3.4 The frozen contract grew three fields

`ROADMAP §3` froze `Input`. We added `Listed`, `Unreadable`, and `Truncated`
after finding that `Load` silently dropped unreadable checkpoints — a repo with
100 unhydrated remote checkpoints reported "no checkpoints in range",
indistinguishable from an empty repo. The freeze existed to protect parallel
work; since the work ended up sequential, nothing was broken by the change.

### 3.5 Databricks was un-cut, then only partly built

`ROADMAP:641` marked Databricks cut. It was reinstated on your instruction, and
the real spec turned out to be `IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md` Step 10 all along.

| Tier | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Delta ingest, keyed `(repo_key, checkpoint_id, session_id)` | **Built** |
| `file://` offline fallback | **Built** (not in the plan; added so the demo needs no workspace) |
| Vector Search over `dead_ends`/`intent` | **Not built** — `ddl.sql` creates only a source view |
| `entire handoff --ask "<task>"` | **Not built** |
| MLflow eval over ~20 labelled pairs | **Not built** |

Transport also diverged: the plan did not specify one; we chose Files API +
`COPY INTO` over generated `INSERT`s so no packet text ever enters a SQL string.

### 3.6 Built solo, not by three people

The roadmap's whole parallelisation design — frozen contract, `stubs.go`, one
owner per file, `ws/spine` / `ws/deadends` / `ws/sections` branches — was built
for three people. The two workstream briefs were written and are accurate, but
no second or third person picked them up. Everything landed on `main` in one
sequence, and `stubs.go` was deleted once every extractor was real.

---

## 4. Two bugs found by running it for real

Both were invisible to the fixtures and only appeared against a repo whose
checkpoints came from upstream.

**Silent skip.** `Load` dropped any checkpoint whose `ReadSessionContent` failed
and said nothing. 100 checkpoints present, "no checkpoints in range" reported —
wrong in exactly the fresh-clone case the command exists for.

**Unbounded walk.** Only successes counted toward `--limit`, so a run with no
readable checkpoints attempted every entry, each a network fetch. Measured:
**over 10 minutes** before being killed. Now bounded by `LoadBudget` (10s) or
`minLoadAttempts`, returning in **13 seconds** and saying it stopped early.

---

## 5. Open, in priority order

1. **No genuine checkpoints exist for this work.** Entire's hooks were installed
   but every invocation skipped with *"not installed or not on PATH"* — the
   binary was only ever at `/tmp/entire`. Now fixed (`/usr/local/bin/entire`,
   `entire doctor` green), but a running agent process cannot pick up hook config
   mid-flight. **Requires a fresh session to start capturing.** Four checkpoints
   are a scored artefact.
2. **`BUILDATHON.md` does not exist.**
3. **Three commits unpushed:** `46fea969e`, `b2684fc1a`, `aaf097182`.
4. **`surface.go` is untested against live graph output** — covered only by an
   injected fake, so the real `entire graph diff` field names are an informed
   guess. Mismatch degrades to the touched-file list rather than breaking.
5. **No graph evidence artefacts captured** — the roadmap requires three.
6. MCP tool, Vector Search, `--ask`, MLflow: not built.

---

## 6. Honest positioning

Against the shipped `session-handoff` skill, three things here are genuinely
new: **dead-end mining from `status:"error"` transcript blocks** (no CLI command
or exported helper surfaces that data today), **line-level citations** that make
each claim resolvable via `entire checkpoint explain`, and **a stable
machine-readable packet**.

The warehouse lane is real but Tier 1 only. Do not describe it as retrieval or
semantic search — it is ingest plus a view shaped for an index that was never
built.

This document breaks down the `entire handoff` implementation plan in both simple English and deep technical terms, so your whole team is on the same page for the pitch and the build.

---

## 🟢 Part 1: The Simple English Version

Essentially, you are building a new command for your CLI called `entire handoff`. Its job is to read the history of what a previous AI agent tried to do, extract the failures, and pass that knowledge to the next AI agent so it doesn't repeat the same mistakes.

Here is your step-by-step game plan:

**1. The Setup (09:15 - 09:35)**
* **What you do:** Fork the main code repository, make sure the Go code compiles locally, and run a quick test.
* **The Goal:** Prove that the logs actually contain the `status:"error"` blocks you need to read. You make a clean "Before" save point (commit) so judges can see where you started.

**2. Building the Skeleton (09:35 - 10:00)**
* **What you do:** You write the basic outer shell of the `entire handoff` command.
* **The Goal:** Make it so that typing `entire handoff` in the terminal actually registers as a command, even if it doesn't do the heavy lifting yet.

**3. Setting up the Blueprint (10:00 - 10:15)**
* **What you do:** You create a structured Go interface (a blueprint called `Packet`).
* **The Goal:** You are splitting the work into smaller "extractors." This is your insurance policy. When the judges throw a surprise requirement at you at noon (the "Curveball"), you can just plug a new extractor into this blueprint without breaking the rest of your code.

**4. The "Dead-End Miner" (The Core Logic)**
* **What you do:** You write the code that scans the raw JSON logs of the previous AI agent's session.
* **The Goal:** Instead of just summarizing the chat, your code specifically hunts for blocks marked `status:"error"`. It grabs exactly what command failed and why, saving it to a list of "dead-ends".

**5. The Output & Databricks Connection**
* **What you do:** You take that list of dead-ends and format it into a clean, machine-readable JSON packet.
* **The Goal:** Instead of giving the next AI a human paragraph to read, you give it structured JSON (which AIs are much better at understanding).
* **The Databricks part:** You use the Databricks Go SDK to send these dead-ends into a Vector Search database. This creates a "global memory"—so if *your* agent fails at something, *my* agent won't try the same thing tomorrow. You then use MLflow to prove this retrieval is accurate.

**6. The Noon Curveball & Final Submission**
* **What you do:** At 12:00, you will get a surprise requirement. Because you built the "blueprint" in step 3, you just add one new Go file to handle the surprise, run your tests, and push the final code by 15:00.

**In one sentence:** You are writing a Go program that reads old AI error logs, saves them to a Databricks brain, and feeds them to new AIs as a clean JSON packet so they stop repeating the same mistakes.

---

## 🔴 Part 2: The Technical Workflow Version

Here is the technical breakdown of the architecture, data pipeline, and execution workflow you are building for the CLI.

### 1. Architectural Overview
You are building a **Cobra-based CLI command** (`entire handoff`) in a fork of `entireio/cli`.

To ensure modularity (and protect against the "Noon Curveball"), the architecture uses the **Strategy Pattern**. Instead of monolithic parsing logic, you define a `handoff.Packet` struct and an `Extractor` interface. Different components (Intent, Dead-Ends, Curveball response) act as independent extractors that mutate the `Packet` concurrently or sequentially.

### 2. The Execution Workflow (Runtime)
When a user (or agent) executes `entire handoff --json`, the following execution flow occurs:

1. **CLI Bootstrap (`cmd/entire/cli/handoff.go`):**
   * The Cobra command parses flags (`--session`, `--json`, `--checkpoint`).
   * It initializes the storage backend by calling `checkpoint.Open(...)`, which returns an `api/checkpoint.PersistentStore` interface.
2. **State Resolution:**
   * The store resolves the requested session/checkpoint ID.
   * It calls `ReadSessionMetadataAndPrompts()` and `ReadSessionContent()` to load the raw blob data from the `.git/refs/entire/checkpoints/` namespace.
3. **The Extractor Pipeline (`packet.go`):**
   * An empty `handoff.Packet` struct is initialized.
   * The command iterates through a slice of registered `Extractor` interfaces (e.g., `IntentExtractor`, `DeadEndMiner`).
   * Each extractor receives the `Context` and the raw session state, executing its isolated logic to populate specific fields in the `Packet`.
4. **Serialization & Stdout:**
   * Based on the `--json` flag, the populated `Packet` is marshaled into a strict, machine-readable JSON schema (resolving issue `#1125`) and dumped to `stdout` for the new agent LLM to ingest.

### 3. The Data Pipeline (The "Dead-End Miner")
This is the core technical complexity of the project.
* **The Constraint:** You cannot use the existing `compact.BuildCondensedEntries` function because it internally discards the `result.status` field when creating the `CondensedEntry` struct. If you touch the `compact` package, you risk breaking 7 other upstream agent sniffers.
* **The Implementation:** Your `DeadEndMiner` extractor reads the raw `transcript.jsonl` bytes directly from the persistent store.
* It parses the v1 JSONL shape (`{v, agent, cli_version, type, ts, id, content[]}`) directly into a custom struct.
* It slices the objects, searching specifically for `content[].result.status == "error"` (which is written by `buildToolResult` when `tr.isError` is true).
* It preserves the exact line offsets (`compact_transcript_start`) to maintain citation integrity.

### 4. The Databricks Subsystem (Global State)
Instead of handoffs being limited to local Git state, you are introducing a globally distributed state using the Databricks Go SDK (`github.com/databricks/databricks-sdk-go`).
* **Write Path:** Once the `DeadEndMiner` finishes parsing local `status:"error"` blocks, it constructs a vector embedding payload and fires an asynchronous upsert via the Go SDK to a **Databricks Vector Search** index.
* **Read Path:** During pipeline execution, a `GlobalMemoryExtractor` uses the Go SDK to query the Vector Search endpoint, passing the current session's `Intent` as the vector query. It retrieves semantically similar dead-ends across the *entire organization's* history and appends them to the `Packet`.
* **Evaluation:** You utilize the Databricks MLflow REST API to track evaluations of this vector retrieval logic locally.

### 5. Git & Integration Workflow
To ship this rapidly in a 2-hour window without merge conflicts:
* **Branching:** You are using independent workstreams (`ws/spine`, `ws/deadends`, `ws/sections`).
* **Integration:** Developer "A" owns the `main` branch. Developers "B" and "C" push their feature branches. "A" merges them locally using `git merge --no-ff` (preserving the commit history for judges) and pushes the final integrated artifact.
* **Build Constraints:** The project requires CGO because of the `tree-sitter` dependency. The build process uses `mise run build` to compile the Go binary before integration testing.

content.text:
Verified. That document describes a **more ambitious system than what we built**, and it also contains some errors. Here's the honest split.

## ✅ Matches what we built

- Cobra command `entire handoff` — **yes**
- `Packet` + `Extractor` interface for curveball insurance — **yes**
- The dead-end miner, and *why* it can't use `compact.BuildCondensedEntries` (it discards `result.status`; 7 sniffers depend on that package) — **exactly right, we verified it**
- Parsing raw `transcript.jsonl`, hunting `content[].result.status == "error"` — **yes**
- Preserving line offsets via `compact_transcript_start` for citation integrity — **yes**
- `checkpoint.Open(...)` → `PersistentStore` — **yes**

The core product description is accurate.

## ❌ Not built, and won't be

**The entire Databricks §4 subsystem.** The doc describes: Databricks Go SDK → vector embeddings → async upsert → a `GlobalMemoryExtractor` that queries Vector Search with your Intent → MLflow evaluation.

**None of that exists.** `grep databricks go.mod` → **0**. There is no SDK, no embedding, no vector query, no `GlobalMemoryExtractor` (that would be a 6th extractor — we have 5), no MLflow.

What we built instead: a **separate binary** that ships packet rows into a Delta table over plain `net/http`, plus a SQL view *shaped* for an index nobody created.

**Why:** the plan's own rule — **stdlib only, no `go.mod` changes** — exists so a `go.sum` conflict can't wreck a late merge. The Databricks SDK violates that directly. It was also scoped as a stretch item and the time went to the core product.

## ⚠️ Built differently

**Extractors don't mutate the Packet.** The doc says they "mutate the `Packet` concurrently or sequentially." Ours each return a `Section`; `Build` assembles them. Pure functions, no shared mutable state — that's why the tests run in milliseconds with no git repo.

**We don't call `ReadSessionMetadataAndPrompts`.** Our `Store` interface is three methods: `List`, `Read`, `ReadSessionContent`. Narrower on purpose, so a small fake covers it.

**Transport is Files API + `COPY INTO`**, not the SDK — so no packet text ever enters a SQL string.

## 🔴 Three factual errors in the doc

1. **"The project requires CGO because of the `tree-sitter` dependency."** **False.** There is no tree-sitter in `go.mod` and no CGO is needed. If you pitch this, someone will check.
2. **`mise run build`** — mise isn't installed on this machine. Everything was built with `go build`.
3. **Workstreams `ws/spine` / `ws/deadends` / `ws/sections`, Devs A/B/C, `--no-ff` merges** — didn't happen. Built solo, sequentially, on `main`.

## 🟡 One real gap it caught

The doc lists `--session` as a flag. **We don't have it** — only `--checkpoint`, `--format`, `--limit`, `--no-graph`, `--json`. That was in the original plan and I dropped it. It's a small addition if you want it.

## What to say in the pitch

Say: reads session recordings, mines failures no existing command surfaces, emits a cited machine-readable packet, and ships it to a Delta table for team-wide history.

**Don't say:** vector search, semantic memory, global memory, embeddings, MLflow, or "the whole organization's history." None of it is real, and `grep databricks go.mod` returning 0 is a fast way for a judge to find that out.

So the Go side never embeds anything — it just POSTs a query string. That keeps us stdlib-only and avoids the `go.mod` churn.

Critically, retrieved rows carry their original `checkpoint_id` and `cite_line`, so **citations survive retrieval** — the product's core claim stays intact.

# What to do next

Handover notes for continuing `entire handoff` on another machine.
Written 2026-09-06 from the macOS box. Everything below is verified, not assumed.

---

## 0. Get the code first — it is NOT pushed

**5 commits exist only on the macOS machine.** Do not start work on Linux until
these are on the remote, or you will duplicate or lose them.

```
b35246429  Add cross-repo retrieval, --ask and --session
20b1d9c59  Record build status, divergences from the plan, and a correction
aaf097182  Add a labelled sample packet for demoing handoff output
b2684fc1a  Verify Entire hooks now capture commits
46fea969e  Bound handoff checkpoint reads and report unreadable ones
```

**Why the push fails — it is a permissions mismatch, not a network problem:**

```
remote: Permission to NiharikaPanda09/cli.git denied to Niharika-Shipthis
```

The repo is owned by **NiharikaPanda09**, but git is authenticating as
**Niharika-Shipthis** (`niharika@shipthis.co`). Two different GitHub accounts.
`git ls-remote` succeeds because reading is allowed; writing is not.

Pick one:

- **Log in as the repo owner** — `gh auth login` as `NiharikaPanda09`, then push.
- **Give `Niharika-Shipthis` write access** to `NiharikaPanda09/cli` on GitHub.
- **Push to a fork you own** — `git remote add mine <url> && git push mine main`.

Nothing else in this list matters until the commits are somewhere you can clone.

---

## 1. Set up the Linux machine

The macOS box needed manual setup and Linux will too. **Neither Go nor mise was
installed here** — I installed Go via brew and put the binary on PATH by hand.

```bash
# Go 1.26.6+ is required (go.mod). Go 1.27.1 was used on macOS and works.
go version

# Build and install the CLI somewhere on PATH.
go build -o ~/.local/bin/entire ./cmd/entire
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"        # add to ~/.bashrc to persist
entire version
```

**This step is not optional and is the single biggest trap.** Entire's git hooks
run `command -v entire`. If the binary is not on PATH, every hook silently
prints *"Entire CLI is enabled but not installed or not on PATH"* and exits —
which is exactly why the first six commits of this project have **no checkpoints
at all**. Verify before doing anything else:

```bash
sh -c 'command -v entire >/dev/null && echo HOOKS-WILL-RUN || echo BROKEN'
```

Then confirm a commit actually records:

```bash
git commit --allow-empty -m "check capture"
git log -1 --format=%B | grep -c "Entire-Checkpoint:"   # must print 1
```

Optional but useful:

```bash
entire plugin install graph      # already installed on macOS, v0.4.0
golangci-lint --version          # needed before pushing; CI enforces it
```

---

## 2. Capture the three graph artefacts — 15 points, minutes of work

**None have been captured.** The graph plugin is installed (v0.4.0) but was
never run. This is the highest value-per-effort item left.

```bash
entire graph init-agents --repo .
# then START A FRESH AGENT SESSION so it picks up the graph instructions

# Artefact 1 — a definition lookup
entire graph def --repo . --symbol runHandoff --format json > graph-1-def.json

# Artefact 2 — impact analysis BEFORE a high-risk change (do it before editing)
entire graph impact --repo . --symbol Load --format json > graph-2-impact.json

# Artefact 3 — semantic diff of the final implementation (do this last)
entire graph diff --repo . --format json > graph-3-diff.json
```

`entire graph impact` **requires `--symbol`** and will not accept a bare file
path. That is why `surface.go` uses `graph diff` instead.

---

## 3. Write `BUILDATHON.md` — required for submission

Does not exist. Use these headings, in this order:

1. **The problem and the intended user.**
2. **Demand citations:** `cli#408`, `#1125`, `#381`, `#985`, `#296`.
3. **Positioning against the shipped `session-handoff` skill.** Not optional —
   `cli#381` was closed pointing at it, and whoever wrote that reply may be
   judging. Name the three things it cannot do: dead-end mining from
   `status:"error"` transcript blocks, graph-scoped blast radius, and the
   machine-readable packet `#1125` asked for by name.
4. **The curveball** — none was issued; say so plainly rather than inventing one.
5. **The three disclosures**, stated in our own words first:
   - Dead ends are **Claude Code only** — other agents produce no usable `transcript.jsonl`.
   - Dead-end grouping is a **heuristic** (exact command / path / tool name).
   - `dependents_count` is a **textual index that can undercount**, emitting
     `W_ANALYSIS_BUDGET_EXCEEDED`.
6. **The `handoff` classification call** — unlisted, read-only, and why.
7. **Links** to the sample packet and any recording.

Full source material is in `docs-private/STATUS_AND_DIVERGENCES.md` — it already
has the divergences, the bugs found, and the honest positioning paragraph.

**Do not claim** vector search, semantic memory, embeddings, MLflow, or "the
whole organisation's history" as working features. See §5.

---

## 4. Finish the Databricks lane (needs a workspace)

The Go side is **done and tested**; only workspace provisioning is left.

```bash
# 1. Apply the DDL — it enables Change Data Feed and adds the row_id key.
#    A Delta Sync index fails with a cryptic error without CDF.
#    File: databricks/ddl.sql

# 2. Create endpoint + index. This is NOT SQL; the exact REST calls are in

#    POST /api/2.0/vector-search/endpoints   {"name":"entire-handoff", ...}
#    POST /api/2.0/vector-search/indexes     {"name":"main.default.handoff_idx", ...}

# 3. Point the CLI at it
export DATABRICKS_HOST=https://<workspace>.cloud.databricks.com
export DATABRICKS_TOKEN=<token>
export DATABRICKS_WAREHOUSE_ID=<id>
export DATABRICKS_VOLUME_PATH=/Volumes/main/default/handoff
export DATABRICKS_VECTOR_INDEX=main.default.handoff_idx

# 4. Ingest and query

entire handoff --ask "how do I mock the checkpoint store"

content.text:
Here's the map — and I found a problem while looking.

## The main code

**`cmd/entire/cli/handoff/`** — the package, ~1,400 lines:

| File | Job |
|---|---|
| `packet.go` | The contract — `Citation`, `Item`, `Section`, `Packet`, `Input`, `Extractor` |
| `input.go` | Walks the checkpoint store, newest first, bounded |
| `build.go` | Runs every extractor, assembles the packet |
| `extractors.go` | The wiring list |
| `intent.go` · `openitems.go` · `stopped.go` | Sections 1, 2, 5 |
| `transcript.go` · `deadends.go` | **The dead-end miner** — the differentiator |
| `surface.go` | Blast radius via `entire graph diff` |
| `globalmemory.go` | Vector Search retrieval (248 lines, the newest piece) |
| `render_md.go` · `render_json.go` | Output |

**`cmd/entire/cli/handoff.go`** (151 lines) — the cobra command and flags.
**`cmd/entire/cli/setup_handoff_skill.go`** (146 lines) — the managed skill.
**`cmd/handoff-databricks/`** — `main.go`, `rows.go`, `upload.go` — the warehouse binary.
**`databricks/ddl.sql`** — table, volume, retrieval view, Vector Search setup.

Plus 4 one-line edits in `root.go`, `agent_help_cmd.go`, `setup.go`, `root_test.go`.

**Total: 3,527 lines across 30 files.**

## The problem I found

A **9.0 MB compiled binary** (`handoff-databricks`, Mach-O arm64) was committed at the repo root in the "first stable session" commit.

Cause: `go build ./...` writes one executable per `main` package into the working directory. `.gitignore` listed `/entire` but not the *second* binary we added, so a `git add -A` swept it in.

Worth flagging beyond the bloat: it's a **macOS arm64 build**, so it wouldn't even run on the Linux machine you're moving to.

Fixed in `80b5fde58` — added `/handoff-databricks` to `.gitignore` and untracked it. File kept on disk.

**The 9 MB blob is still in git history.** Removing it entirely needs another `filter-branch` + force-push. Given you just did one and it went cleanly, it's low-risk — but it's your call whether it's worth the churn. Want me to purge it, or leave it?

Also still unpushed: the last two commits.
